did_you_know.text: The heading presents the psalm as a musical composition: it is intended for the director of music, associated with the gittith, and attributed to Asaph. The meaning of the term “upon the Gittith” is not explicitly explained in the verse.
The psalm opens with a call to rejoice and shout for joy to the God of Jacob, presenting praise as a public response of the people of Israel.
The verses list several musical instruments—the tambourine, lyre, and harp—and emphasize that worship is offered with singing, music, and joyful shouting.

The psalm commands the blowing of the ram’s horn “at the New Moon” and “at the full moon,” that is, at a festival associated with the beginning of the month or the covered moon. The words “on our feast day” connect the blowing with a national celebration.
The blowing of the ram’s horn is described as “a statute for Israel” and “an ordinance of the God of Jacob”—a binding command and tradition belonging to the people and their heritage.
The verse mentions Joseph and his departure from Egypt, then continues by describing release from forced labor: the burden is removed from the shoulder, and the hands no longer carry the basket.

The Lord describes rescuing Israel in a time of trouble: the people called to him, and he delivered them. The verse also mentions “the secret place of thunder” and “the waters of Meribah,” recalling times of testing in the wilderness.
At the center of the psalm is a call to listen: Israel is urged to hear the Lord’s voice, not to worship a foreign god or bow down to an unfamiliar deity.

The Lord presents himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt and adds the promise, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it”—an expression of confidence that he can provide for his people’s needs.

According to the psalm, the people did not listen to the Lord or obey him. As a result, he gave them over to “the stubbornness of their hearts” and to their own counsels, allowing them to follow their own ways.
The psalm presents a clear condition for blessing: if Israel would listen to the Lord and walk in his ways, he would quickly subdue its enemies and turn his hand against its foes.
The psalm concludes by describing the abundance promised to Israel when it listens to the Lord: rich food, “the finest wheat,” and even honey, poetically described as coming from the rock.
